data.title: Doxycycline
data.summary: II Antibiotics — a) Tetracyclines · Second-generation semisynthetic tetracycline (lipophilic)
data.body:
_Oral · II Antibiotics — a) Tetracyclines_

**Class:** Second-generation semisynthetic tetracycline (lipophilic)

## Mechanism of action
- Antibacterial: binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA attachment → stops protein synthesis (bacteriostatic)
- Anti-inflammatory (independent of antibacterial action): inhibits matrix metalloproteinases, neutrophil chemotaxis, and pro-inflammatory cytokines
- This anti-inflammatory action is the basis of sub-antimicrobial dosing in rosacea

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed (about 95%); food reduces absorption only slightly, but iron, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc and bismuth chelate it
- Half-life 18–22 h → once- or twice-daily dosing
- Excreted mainly through the gut, so it is the safest tetracycline in renal failure

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne vulgaris (moderate–severe inflammatory) — always with topical benzoyl peroxide or retinoid; limit to 3–4 months
- Rosacea (papulopustular), perioral dermatitis
- Bullous pemphigoid (anti-inflammatory, often with nicotinamide)
- STIs: chlamydia/NGU, LGV, donovanosis, early and late syphilis when penicillin cannot be used
- Community MRSA skin infections, Lyme disease, rickettsial infections, Mycobacterium marinum
- Hidradenitis suppurativa; filariasis (kills Wolbachia); confluent and reticulated papillomatosis

## Dose & formulations
- Acne/rosacea: 50–100 mg once or twice daily
- Sub-antimicrobial: 40 mg modified-release once daily, or 20 mg twice daily (rosacea)
- Chlamydia/NGU: 100 mg twice daily × 7 days; LGV: 100 mg twice daily × 21 days
- Early syphilis (penicillin allergy): 100 mg twice daily × 14 days; late latent: × 28 days
- Donovanosis: 100 mg twice daily for at least 3 weeks and until lesions heal
- Take with a full glass of water, sitting upright, not at bedtime

## Adverse effects
- GI upset; pill oesophagitis (take upright with water)
- Phototoxicity, including photo-onycholysis — the most phototoxic of the commonly used tetracyclines
- Tooth staining and enamel hypoplasia in children under 8 years (less than older tetracyclines)
- Pseudotumor cerebri; vaginal candidiasis
- Rare: hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (after about 15 weeks) and breastfeeding (long courses)
- Children under 8 years (except short courses for serious infections such as rickettsial disease)
- Concurrent isotretinoin or acitretin; known hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Antacids, iron, calcium, zinc, magnesium, bismuth, milk: reduce absorption — separate by 2–3 h
- Isotretinoin/acitretin: pseudotumor cerebri
- Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, barbiturates: lower doxycycline levels
- Warfarin: effect may increase

## Monitoring
- No routine blood tests for courses used in acne
- Counsel about sun protection and correct swallowing

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (old FDA category D): tooth discolouration and bone effects after about 15 weeks. Short courses in breastfeeding are generally acceptable; avoid long courses.

## Viva points
- Safest tetracycline in renal failure (gut excretion)
- Most phototoxic of the common tetracyclines; photo-onycholysis
- Sub-antimicrobial 40 mg MR works by anti-inflammatory action and does not select resistance
- Never combine with isotretinoin

## Note on sources
Khopkar says doxycycline lacks the anti-inflammatory effect of tetracycline. Wolverton describes clear anti-inflammatory actions (the basis of sub-antimicrobial dosing). We follow Wolverton.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9 (Systemic antibacterial agents); Khopkar ch.1. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
